title: Deep-Dive Literature Review Chain
problem: Synthesizing a pile of papers or sources into a coherent, trustworthy overview is slow by hand and unreliable in one shot — a single mega-prompt over dozens of sources tends to blur distinct findings together, invent citations, and flatten disagreements between sources into false consensus.

workflow.detail: Before touching sources, define the research question and its boundaries with the model: what's in scope, what's explicitly excluded, and what would count as a satisfying answer.
Paste abstracts or key excerpts (not full papers yet) and ask the model to cluster them into 3–6 themes, flagging any source that seems weak, off-topic, or contradictory.
For each theme, feed in the actual source text and ask for claims, supporting evidence, and stated limitations — one theme per prompt, so context doesn't get diluted.
Run the Prompt Template below with all theme summaries as input, asking the model to reconcile agreements, disagreements, and gaps across themes.

Check every citation and claim in the output against the original source text yourself before you trust or publish it. This step is not optional — treat model citations as claims to verify, not facts.
Once verified, ask the model to compose the polished write-up using only the claims you've confirmed.

promptTemplate:
You are a research analyst helping synthesize literature on {{TOPIC}}.

CONTEXT:
{{CONTEXT}}

I have gathered sources organized into these themes:
{{THEMES}}

OBJECTIVE:
{{OBJECTIVE}}

For each theme:
1. Summarize the consensus view in 2-3 sentences.
2. Note any contradicting findings and who holds them.
3. Identify one open question or gap.

Then write a 200-word cross-theme synthesis that connects the themes to the objective above. Cite sources using the format (Author, Year) exactly as given in the theme notes — do not invent citations or infer authors not present in my input.

variables.name: TOPIC
variables.label: Research Topic
variables.placeholder: e.g. Retrieval-augmented generation for code search

variables.name: CONTEXT
variables.label: Context / why this matters
variables.placeholder: e.g. Scoping a technical decision for our search infra

variables.name: THEMES
variables.label: Themes with source notes
variables.placeholder:
Theme 1: Chunking strategies — (Lee, 2023) found...
Theme 2: Reranking — (Ma, 2024) found...

variables.name: OBJECTIVE
variables.label: What the synthesis should conclude toward
variables.placeholder: e.g. A recommendation on chunking strategy for our codebase

exampleOutput:
### Theme: Chunking Strategies
Consensus: Fixed-size chunking underperforms semantic/AST-aware chunking for code retrieval (Lee, 2023; Patel, 2023).
Contradiction: Patel (2023) finds diminishing returns above 512 tokens; Lee (2023) reports gains up to 1024.
Gap: Neither study tests multi-language repos.

### Cross-Theme Synthesis
Across chunking and reranking literature, the strongest gains for code search come from combining AST-aware chunking with a lightweight reranker (Lee, 2023; Ma, 2024)...
tips: Never let the model fetch or browse papers it wasn't given — always paste the actual abstract or excerpt text so it can't hallucinate a citation.
Gemini's long context window is well-suited to Step 3 — dump full paper text rather than just abstracts when doing the per-cluster deep read.
For local LLMs (Ollama) with small context windows, keep the per-theme extraction calls short and run more of them rather than one giant context dump.
Run the human verification pass line by line against the source text — this recipe fails silently if you skip it.
